stem: What must you do when you come to this sign?
choices: Slow down and let traffic on the other road go first, stopping only if needed
Stop only if a police officer is present
Come to a full stop every time, even if no one is coming
Speed up to merge ahead of the other traffic
oneLineConcept: Yield sign: slow down, give way, stop only if needed
explanation:
This red and white triangle with its point at the bottom is the **YIELD** sign. **Slow down** and **give the right of way** to traffic on the road you are entering. If that traffic is close, **stop and wait** for it to pass.

**Wrong choices**
- Come to a full stop every time, even if no one is coming: A full stop every time is required at a STOP sign, not a YIELD sign.
- Speed up to merge ahead of the other traffic: Speeding up to cut in front of traffic is the opposite of yielding.
- Stop only if a police officer is present: The sign applies at all times, whether or not an officer is there.
imageAlt: A sign shaped like a triangle with one point at the bottom. It has a wide red border, a white center, and red capital letters across the top part.

imageSource.title: MUTCD (FHWA) sign R1-2
imageSource.license: U.S. federal government work, public domain

stem: What does this sign tell you to do?
choices: Keep to the right of the island or obstacle ahead
Traffic will merge from the right
Turn right at the next intersection
oneLineConcept: Keep Right sign: pass to the right of the island
explanation:
This white rule sign shows an arrow going around the **right side** of a dark island. It means **keep to the right** of the median, island, or obstacle ahead. Because it is a white rectangle, it is a **rule you must obey**.

**Wrong choices**
- Turn right at the next intersection: A turn sign would show an arrow bending sharply to the right, not passing an obstacle.
- The right lane ends ahead: A lane-ending warning is a yellow diamond, not a white rectangle.
- Traffic will merge from the right: A merge warning is a yellow diamond showing a lane joining the road.
imageAlt: An upright white rectangular sign with a black border. On the left is a tall black oval shape. A thick black arrow starts at the bottom, angles to the right of the oval, and points straight up.

imageSource.title: MUTCD (FHWA) sign R4-7
imageSource.license: U.S. federal government work, public domain

stem: What does this sign mean?
choices: The road curves to the left ahead
Left turns are allowed only on a green arrow
You may not turn left here
oneLineConcept: Red circle and slash over a left arrow: no left turn
explanation:
A **red circle with a slash** means the action shown is **not allowed**. Here the symbol is a **left-turn arrow**, so you **may not turn left** at this place.

**Wrong choices**
- Left turns are allowed only on a green arrow: The sign does not mention signals or arrows; it forbids the turn.
- The road curves to the left ahead: A curve warning is a yellow diamond, not a white square with a red circle.
- Left lane must turn left: A lane-use sign shows arrows over lanes without a red circle and slash.
imageAlt: A white square sign with a black border. A black arrow goes up and then bends to the left. A red circle surrounds the arrow, and a red diagonal line crosses over it from the upper left to the lower right.

imageSource.title: MUTCD (FHWA) sign R3-2

stem: Which sign shape is used only for STOP signs?
oneLineConcept: Eight-sided octagon = STOP only
explanation:
The **octagon**, a sign with **eight sides**, is used **only for STOP signs**. You can know it is a STOP sign from its shape even from behind or when it is covered with snow.

**Wrong choices**
- Triangle: The triangle with its point down is used for YIELD.
- Diamond: Diamonds are used for warning signs.
- Pentagon (five sides): The five-sided shape is used for school zone and school crossing signs.

stem: What colors are used on a YIELD sign?
oneLineConcept: YIELD sign: red and white triangle
explanation:
The YIELD sign is a **triangle** with its point at the bottom, colored **red and white**, with the word YIELD in large letters.

**Wrong choices**
- Black and yellow: Black on yellow is used for general warning signs.
- Green and white: Green and white is used for guide signs that give directions.
- Orange and black: Black on orange is used for work zone signs.

stem: When you reach a STOP sign, what does the law require?
choices: Slow down and roll through if no one is coming
Come to a full stop and go only when the way is clear
Stop only if there are pedestrians
oneLineConcept: STOP sign: full stop every time
explanation:
At a STOP sign the law requires a **full stop**. Do not move again until you are **sure the way is clear**.

**Wrong choices**
- Slow down and roll through if no one is coming: Rolling through without stopping is illegal even if the road looks empty.
- Stop only if there are pedestrians: You must stop whether or not people are crossing.
- Stop only at night: The sign applies at every hour of the day.

stem: At an intersection with a STOP sign but no stop line and no marked crosswalk, where should you stop?
choices: In the middle of the intersection
Before entering the intersection, where you can see the cross street
Right beside the STOP sign, even if you cannot see
oneLineConcept: No stop line or crosswalk: stop where you can see cross traffic
explanation:
Stop at a marked stop line if there is one. If there is **no stop line or marked crosswalk**, stop **before entering the intersection** at a point where you **can see the intersecting street**.

**Wrong choices**
- In the middle of the intersection: Stopping inside the intersection blocks cross traffic and is unsafe.
- Right beside the STOP sign, even if you cannot see: The goal is to stop where you can see; the sign's exact spot does not matter if your view is blocked.
- Fifty feet before the sign: There is no rule to stop fifty feet before the sign.

stem: What kind of information do white rectangular signs with black letters usually give?
choices: Traffic rules you must obey, such as speed limits
oneLineConcept: White rectangles: rule (regulatory) signs
explanation:
Rectangular and square signs that are **black and white** (or red and white) show **speed limits and other rules**, such as NO U-TURN. Failing to obey them is a **traffic violation**.

**Wrong choices**
- Directions to cities: Directions to cities are shown on green guide signs.
- Nearby hospitals and gas stations: Services such as hospitals are shown on blue signs.
- Hazards ahead, such as curves: Hazards ahead are shown on yellow diamond warning signs.

stem: What does a red circle with a slash over a symbol mean?
choices: The action shown is not allowed
The action shown is allowed only at night
oneLineConcept: Red circle with slash: the action is not allowed
explanation:
A **red circle with a slash** over a symbol means the action in the symbol is **prohibited**, such as a left turn or a U-turn.

**Wrong choices**
- The action shown is allowed only at night: The sign does not limit the rule to certain hours.
- The action shown is recommended: A slash forbids the action; it does not recommend it.
- There is a hazard ahead: Hazards ahead are shown on yellow diamond warning signs.

stem: You are stopped at a steady red light and want to turn right. There is no sign about turning. What may you do?
choices: Wait for the green light, because turns on red are never allowed
Turn right only if a green arrow appears
Turn right after a complete stop, yielding to traffic and pedestrians
Turn right without stopping if the road is clear
oneLineConcept: Right on red: allowed after a full stop unless a sign forbids
explanation:
Unless a **NO TURN ON RED** sign is posted, you may **turn right on a steady red light** after a **complete stop**. You must **yield** to other traffic and to pedestrians using or starting to cross the intersection.

**Wrong choices**
- Turn right without stopping if the road is clear: You must come to a complete stop before turning on red.
- Wait for the green light, because turns on red are never allowed: Right turns on red are allowed unless a sign forbids them.
- Turn right only if a green arrow appears: A green arrow is not needed for a right turn on red after a full stop.

stem: A sign reads KEEP RIGHT EXCEPT TO PASS. What does it mean on a highway with two or more lanes your way?
choices: Trucks must use the right lane, but cars may use any lane
Passing is not allowed on this road
Drive in the left lane unless you are turning right
Stay in the right lane and use the left lane only to pass
oneLineConcept: KEEP RIGHT EXCEPT TO PASS: left lane is for passing
explanation:
This black and white **rule sign** means you should **drive in the right lane** and use the **left lane only to pass**. North Carolina also says slower drivers on multi-lane highways should stay in the right lane unless passing or turning left.

**Wrong choices**
- Drive in the left lane unless you are turning right: The sign says the opposite: keep right, not left.
- Passing is not allowed on this road: The sign allows passing; it tells you which lane to pass in.
- Trucks must use the right lane, but cars may use any lane: The sign applies to all drivers, not only to trucks.

stem: The handbook says a STOP sign is usually posted how far from the intersection?
oneLineConcept: STOP sign usually 6 to 50 feet from the intersection
explanation:
The **STOP sign** is usually posted **6 to 50 feet** from the intersection. Because it can be some distance from the cross street, stop where the stop line, crosswalk, or your view of the cross street tells you to.

**Wrong choices**
- 100 to 200 feet: The handbook gives 6 to 50 feet, which is much closer than this.
- Exactly 10 feet: The handbook gives a range of 6 to 50 feet, not one fixed distance.
- 300 to 500 feet: The handbook gives 6 to 50 feet, which is much closer than this.

stem: You approach a YIELD sign and traffic on the cross road is close. What should you do?
choices: Stop and wait for the traffic to pass before you enter
Speed up to enter the gap quickly
Go first because you reached the sign first
Sound your horn and enter slowly
oneLineConcept: Yield: stop and wait if cross traffic is close
explanation:
At a **YIELD** sign you must slow down and **give the right of way**. Whether you stop depends on the other traffic. If it is close, **stop and wait** for it to pass so you do not interfere with it.

**Wrong choices**
- Go first because you reached the sign first: Reaching the sign first does not give you the right of way.
- Sound your horn and enter slowly: The horn does not give you permission to enter in front of traffic.
- Speed up to enter the gap quickly: Speeding up into a small gap forces other drivers to brake.

stem: A parking space has a sign with the wheelchair symbol. What does it mean?
choices: The space is reserved for vehicles with a disability plate or placard
Parking for anyone for up to 15 minutes
oneLineConcept: Handicap parking: only with a disability plate or placard
explanation:
The **handicap parking sign** shows that a space is **reserved** for people who qualify and **display a handicap license plate or a dashboard placard**. Parking there without one is against the law.

**Wrong choices**
- Parking for delivery vans only: The sign does not set aside the space for deliveries.
- Parking for anyone for up to 15 minutes: The sign does not allow short-term parking for others.
- A hospital is nearby: Hospitals are shown on blue service signs along the road, not on parking space signs.

stem: You are stopped at a red light where a NO TURN ON RED sign is posted. Cross traffic and pedestrians are clear. What must you do before turning right?
choices: Turn only if the driver behind you honks
Turn after slowing down because no one is coming
Turn after a full stop because the way is clear
Wait until the light turns green
oneLineConcept: NO TURN ON RED: wait for green even if clear
explanation:
A **NO TURN ON RED** sign takes away the usual right-on-red rule. Even when the way is clear, you must **wait for the green light** before turning.

**Wrong choices**
- Turn after a full stop because the way is clear: A full stop is enough only when no sign forbids turning on red.
- Turn after slowing down because no one is coming: Slowing down is never enough on a red light; here you may not turn at all.
- Turn only if the driver behind you honks: Another driver's horn does not change the sign's rule.

stem: Which statement about regulatory signs is NOT correct?
choices: They tell you about laws you must obey
Speed limit signs are regulatory signs
Ignoring them is a violation of traffic law
oneLineConcept: Regulatory signs are rectangles or squares, not yellow diamonds
explanation:
Regulatory signs state **rules you must obey**, such as speed limits. They are usually **rectangles or squares in black and white or red and white**. **Yellow diamonds are warning signs**, so that statement is the one that is not correct.

**Wrong choices**
- They tell you about laws you must obey: This is correct: regulatory signs state traffic laws.
- Speed limit signs are regulatory signs: This is correct: a speed limit sign is a regulatory sign.
- Ignoring them is a violation of traffic law: This is correct: failing to obey them breaks traffic law.

stem: You see an octagon-shaped sign from behind as you approach an intersection on the cross road. What can you tell?
choices: Traffic on the other road must stop there
Traffic on the other road must yield
Your road has a school zone
oneLineConcept: Octagon shape seen from behind is still a STOP sign
explanation:
Only STOP signs are **octagons**, so you can tell from the **shape alone**, even from the back, that drivers on that road **must stop**. This helps you predict what other drivers should do, but still watch for anyone who does not stop.

**Wrong choices**
- Traffic on the other road must yield: A yield sign is a triangle, not an octagon.
- Your road has a school zone: School signs have five sides, not eight.
- A railroad crossing is ahead: Railroad advance warning signs are round.

stem: What does this five-sided sign warn you about?
choices: A pedestrian mall where cars are not allowed
A school zone or school crossing
oneLineConcept: Five-sided sign: school zone or school crossing
explanation:
The **five-sided (pentagon) sign** warns of a **school zone or school crossing**. Watch closely for **children**, and remember that in many school zones the **speed limit is lower** during school hours.

**Wrong choices**
- A playground for adults: The five-sided shape is used for schools, not adult play areas.
- A hospital zone: Hospitals are shown on blue service signs.
- A pedestrian mall where cars are not allowed: This sign warns of children crossing; it does not close the road to cars.
imageAlt: A yellow-green sign with five sides, shaped like a house with a pointed top. It shows two black figures of children walking side by side, one taller than the other.

imageSource.title: MUTCD (FHWA) sign S1-1
imageSource.license: U.S. federal government work, public domain

stem: What does this yellow warning sign mean?
choices: You are entering a one-way street
Traffic ahead moves in both directions on the same road
Two lanes going your way are ahead
Passing is allowed in both lanes ahead
oneLineConcept: Two-way traffic sign: oncoming traffic shares the road
explanation:
The two arrows point in **opposite directions**, so the sign warns that **traffic moves both ways** ahead. You will share the road with **oncoming vehicles**, so stay on your side.

**Wrong choices**
- You are entering a one-way street: A one-way street is marked with a black and white ONE WAY sign.
- Two lanes going your way are ahead: Two lanes going the same way would show arrows pointing the same way.
- Passing is allowed in both lanes ahead: The sign shows opposite traffic; it does not say passing is allowed.
imageAlt: A yellow diamond-shaped sign with a black border. It shows two thick black vertical arrows side by side. The left arrow points down and the right arrow points up.

imageSource.title: MUTCD (FHWA) sign W6-3
imageSource.license: U.S. federal government work, public domain

stem: What does this yellow warning sign mean?
choices: The road has sharp curves for several miles
The road is slippery when wet
Loose gravel may hit your windshield
oneLineConcept: Car with wavy tracks: slippery when wet
explanation:
The sign shows a **car with wavy skid marks** behind it. It warns that the road is **slippery when wet**. In rain, **slow down**, increase your following distance, and avoid sudden braking or steering.

**Wrong choices**
- A car wash is ahead: Businesses such as car washes are not marked with warning signs.
- The road has sharp curves for several miles: Curves are shown with a curved arrow, not a car with skid marks.
- Loose gravel may hit your windshield: This sign is about traction on a wet road, not flying gravel.
imageAlt: A yellow diamond-shaped sign with a black border. It shows the back of a black car with two wavy black lines trailing below it, one under each rear wheel.

imageSource.title: MUTCD (FHWA) sign W8-5
imageSource.license: U.S. federal government work, public domain

stem: What shape are most warning signs?
oneLineConcept: Warning signs are diamond-shaped
explanation:
Most warning signs are **diamonds**, normally **black on yellow**. They warn of a **hazard or change** in the road ahead.

**Wrong choices**
- Octagon: The octagon is used only for STOP.
- Circle: The round sign is used for the railroad advance warning.
- Upright rectangle: Upright rectangles are mostly used for rule signs, such as speed limits.

stem: What does an orange diamond-shaped sign with black letters tell you?
choices: A construction or maintenance work zone is ahead
The speed limit is about to rise
oneLineConcept: Orange signs: work zones
explanation:
**Orange signs with black messages** are used only for **work zones**. When you see one, **stay alert**, slow down, and be ready for lane shifts, workers, and flaggers.

**Wrong choices**
- A school zone is ahead: School signs are yellow-green with five sides.
- A rest area is ahead: Rest areas are shown on guide signs.
- The speed limit is about to rise: Speed limits are shown on white rule signs.

stem: What does a round yellow sign with a black X and the letters RR mean?
oneLineConcept: Round yellow RR sign: railroad crossing ahead
explanation:
The **round yellow sign** with an **X and RR** gives **advance warning of a railroad crossing**. **Slow down**, look and listen, and be ready to stop.

**Wrong choices**
- Road repairs are ahead: Road work is shown with orange work zone signs.
- Right lane closed: A lane closure is shown on a diamond or rectangular sign with words or lane symbols.
- A rest room is nearby: Rest rooms are shown on blue service or guide signs.

stem: Where is the X-shaped crossbuck sign placed?
choices: About a mile before the railroad crossing
oneLineConcept: Crossbuck: at the railroad crossing itself
explanation:
The **crossbuck** is a white X-shaped sign reading RAILROAD CROSSING. It stands **at the crossing itself**. A smaller sign below it shows if there is **more than one track**.

**Wrong choices**
- About a mile before the railroad crossing: The round yellow RR sign is the advance warning before the crossing.
- Only at crossings with gates: Crossbucks are used at crossings with or without gates.
- On the train: The sign stands beside the road, not on the train.

stem: What does a yellow STOP AHEAD warning sign tell you?
choices: A STOP sign is ahead that may be hard to see
You must stop at this sign
oneLineConcept: STOP AHEAD: a hidden STOP sign is coming
explanation:
**STOP AHEAD** is a warning sign placed well before a STOP sign when a **curve or other objects block your view** of it. Begin **slowing down** so you can stop at the STOP sign.

**Wrong choices**
- You must stop at this sign: The warning sign itself is not where you stop; you stop at the STOP sign.
- A police checkpoint is ahead: The sign warns of a STOP sign, not a checkpoint.
- The road ends: A road that ends has its own warning sign.

stem: On which side of the road is the yellow no-passing pennant posted?
choices: On either side, depending on the county
Above the center of the road
oneLineConcept: No-passing pennant: left side of the road
explanation:
The yellow **pennant** is posted on the **left side of the road**, where a driver about to pass will see it. It **points to where the no-passing zone begins**, where a solid yellow line starts in your lane.

**Wrong choices**
- The right side: The DO NOT PASS rule sign is on the right; the pennant is on the left.
- Above the center of the road: The pennant is mounted at the roadside, not over the road.
- On either side, depending on the county: Its placement does not change by county.

stem: What shape is the warning sign that marks the start of a no-passing zone?
choices: A pennant (a long triangle on its side)
oneLineConcept: No-passing zone sign: yellow pennant
explanation:
The **no-passing zone** sign is a yellow **pennant**, a long triangle lying on its side. It **adds emphasis** to the rectangular DO NOT PASS rule sign.

**Wrong choices**
- A diamond: Diamonds are used for most other warning signs.
- A circle: The circle is used for the railroad advance warning.
- A pentagon: The pentagon is used for school signs.

stem: In a work zone, a flagger holds up a paddle that says STOP. What should you do?
choices: Slow down and go around the flagger
Stop and wait until the flagger signals you to go
Stop only if you see workers on the road
oneLineConcept: Flagger's STOP paddle: stop and wait
explanation:
Work zone flaggers use a **STOP/SLOW paddle** to control traffic. When the paddle shows **STOP**, you must **stop and wait** until the flagger lets you go.

**Wrong choices**
- Slow down and go around the flagger: Driving around a flagger who shows STOP is dangerous and illegal.
- Stop only if you see workers on the road: The flagger's signal applies whether or not you can see workers.
- Honk and continue slowly: Honking does not give you permission to go.

stem: Where does a highway work zone begin and end?
choices: It begins at the first cone and ends at the last worker
From the first sign marking the start of the work zone to the last sign marking its end
Within 500 feet of any construction equipment
Only where workers are present that day
oneLineConcept: Work zone: from the first sign to the last sign
explanation:
A highway work zone is the area **between the first sign** that shows the **start** of the work zone and the **last sign** that shows its **end**. The posted work zone speed limit applies in that whole area.

**Wrong choices**
- It begins at the first cone and ends at the last worker: Cones and workers do not set the legal limits; the signs do.
- Only where workers are present that day: The work zone exists even when no workers are visible.
- Within 500 feet of any construction equipment: There is no fixed 500-foot rule; the signs mark the zone.

stem: You see a yellow diamond with black symbols and then an orange diamond with black symbols. What is the difference?
choices: Both are warnings, but orange ones warn of construction or maintenance work
Yellow signs are rules; orange signs are suggestions
Orange signs are for trucks only
Yellow signs apply only at night
oneLineConcept: Yellow diamond: general warning; orange: work zone warning
explanation:
Both are **warning signs** with the diamond shape. **Black on yellow** warns of general hazards, while **black on orange** warns of **construction or maintenance areas**, so drive with extra care.

**Wrong choices**
- Yellow signs are rules; orange signs are suggestions: Neither color is a rule sign; both are warnings you should heed.
- Orange signs are for trucks only: Orange work zone signs apply to all drivers.
- Yellow signs apply only at night: Yellow warning signs apply at all hours.

stem: Which of these is NOT shown on a five-sided (pentagon) sign?
oneLineConcept: Railroad advance warning is round, not five-sided
explanation:
The **five-sided sign** warns of a **school zone or school crossing**, where children may be present. A **railroad crossing ahead** is shown by a **round** yellow sign with an X and RR, not a pentagon.

**Wrong choices**
- School zone: This is shown on a five-sided sign.
- School crossing: This is shown on a five-sided sign.
- Children near a school: The five-sided sign warns that schoolchildren may be present.

stem: You are about to pass on a two-lane road and see a yellow pennant on the left side. What should you do?
choices: Pass only if the car ahead is going under the speed limit
Finish passing quickly before the solid line starts
Move into the left lane and wait there
Do not start to pass, because a no-passing zone begins
oneLineConcept: Pennant: do not start a pass into a no-passing zone
explanation:
The pennant **points to the start of a no-passing zone**, where a **solid yellow line** begins on your side. **Do not begin a pass** that you cannot finish before that point.

**Wrong choices**
- Finish passing quickly before the solid line starts: Rushing to pass at the start of a no-passing zone is dangerous and illegal.
- Pass only if the car ahead is going under the speed limit: A slower car ahead does not make it legal to pass in a no-passing zone.
- Move into the left lane and wait there: Driving in the oncoming lane while waiting is very dangerous.

stem: What does the small sign under a railroad crossbuck show?
choices: That there is more than one track
The speed of the next train
The time of the next train
oneLineConcept: Sign under the crossbuck: number of tracks
explanation:
A smaller sign **below the crossbuck** shows when there is **more than one track** at the crossing. After one train passes, **another may be coming** on a different track.

**Wrong choices**
- The speed of the next train: Train speed is not posted at crossings.
- The name of the railroad: The railroad's name and an emergency number appear on the blue emergency sign, not under the crossbuck.
- The time of the next train: Train schedules are not posted on crossing signs.

stem: What shape is the route marker for a North Carolina state highway?
oneLineConcept: North Carolina route markers are diamonds
explanation:
**North Carolina route markers are diamond-shaped**. U.S. highways use a **shield**, and Interstates use a **red, white, and blue shield**.

**Wrong choices**
- Shield: The shield is used for U.S. highways and, in red, white, and blue, for Interstates.
- Circle: A circle is not the North Carolina route marker.
- Triangle: The triangle with its point down is the YIELD sign.

stem: What do blue and white signs along the highway show?
choices: Services such as a hospital or a Highway Patrol station
oneLineConcept: Blue and white signs: services
explanation:
**Blue and white** signs point to **services**, such as a **hospital**, a **Highway Patrol station**, or a telephone.

**Wrong choices**
- Construction work ahead: Construction work is shown on orange signs.
- Speed limits: Speed limits are shown on white rule signs.
- Railroad crossings: Railroad crossings are shown on yellow round signs and white crossbucks.

stem: Which route marker is a red, white, and blue shield?
oneLineConcept: Red, white, and blue shield: Interstate
explanation:
**Interstate highways** are marked by a **red, white, and blue shield**. U.S. highways use a plain shield, and North Carolina routes use a diamond.

**Wrong choices**
- U.S. highway: U.S. highways use a shield, but not the red, white, and blue Interstate shield.
- North Carolina secondary road: North Carolina secondary road signs are rectangles.
- County road: This shield is reserved for the Interstate system.

stem: What do green guide signs tell you?
oneLineConcept: Green guide signs: directions and distances
explanation:
**Green guide signs** give **directions, route numbers, and distances** to places. If you are lost, a mileage and direction sign can help you.

**Wrong choices**
- Warnings about curves: Curves are shown on yellow warning signs.
- Speed limits: Speed limits are shown on white rule signs.
- Where you may not park: Parking rules are shown on rule signs, not green guide signs.

stem: Which direction does an even-numbered highway generally run?
choices: In a circle around a city
oneLineConcept: Even numbers: east-west; odd numbers: north-south
explanation:
**Even-numbered highways** generally run **east and west**. **Odd-numbered highways** generally run **north and south**.

**Wrong choices**
- North and south: North-south routes generally have odd numbers.
- In a circle around a city: Loop routes around cities exist, but even numbers generally mean east-west routes.
- It depends on the county: The numbering pattern is the same in every county.

stem: What shape are North Carolina secondary road signs?
oneLineConcept: NC secondary road signs are rectangles
explanation:
**North Carolina secondary road signs are rectangular**. The **diamond** is used for North Carolina numbered routes, and the **shield** for U.S. highways.

**Wrong choices**
- Diamond: The diamond marks North Carolina routes, not secondary roads.
- Shield: The shield marks U.S. and Interstate highways.
- Pentagon: The pentagon is the school sign.

stem: You are lost and want to read a guide sign. What is the safe thing to do?
choices: Back up to the last sign you passed
Stop in your lane to read the sign
Slow to a crawl in the left lane
Pull onto the shoulder when it is safe, then figure out your route
oneLineConcept: Lost? Pull onto the shoulder safely, never stop in the road
explanation:
Do **not** stop in the road to read a sign, because other drivers may hit you. When it is **safe, move to the shoulder**, stop, and work out where you are and which way to go.

**Wrong choices**
- Stop in your lane to read the sign: Stopping in a travel lane can cause a rear-end crash.
- Slow to a crawl in the left lane: Very slow driving in the passing lane is dangerous.
- Back up to the last sign you passed: Backing up on a highway is very dangerous.

stem: A highway is numbered with an odd number. Which way does it generally run?
oneLineConcept: Odd-numbered highways run north and south
explanation:
**Odd-numbered highways** generally run **north and south**, and **even-numbered highways** generally run **east and west**.

**Wrong choices**
- East and west: East-west routes generally have even numbers.
- Only along the coast: Route numbers are used across the whole state, not only the coast.
- Only through cities: Odd numbers are used on rural roads as well as city roads.

stem: At a railroad crossing you see a blue sign with a phone number, a crossing number, and the railroad's name. What is it for?
choices: Reporting an emergency or a problem with the crossing to the railroad
Calling to ask when the next train will come
Paying a fine for a crossing violation
oneLineConcept: Blue ENS sign: report railroad emergencies
explanation:
This is the **Emergency Notification System (ENS) sign**, often called the **blue sign**. It shows the **crossing ID number**, the **railroad name**, and a **phone number** to report an emergency, a stalled vehicle, or broken lights or gates directly to the railroad.

**Wrong choices**
- Calling to ask when the next train will come: The number is for emergencies and problems, not train schedules.
- Paying a fine for a crossing violation: Fines are not paid through this sign.
- Finding the nearest gas station: Gas stations are shown on blue service signs along highways, not at crossings.

stem: Which of these is NOT a color used for guide signs?
oneLineConcept: Guide signs: green, brown, or blue; red is for stop and yield
explanation:
Guide signs are rectangles that may be **green, brown, or blue**. **Red** is used for signs such as **STOP and YIELD**, which are rule signs, not guide signs.

**Wrong choices**
- Green: Green is used for guide signs that give directions and distances.
- Brown: Brown is used for guide signs to parks and recreation areas.
- Blue: Blue is used for guide signs that show services.

stem: You see a diamond-shaped route marker and a shield-shaped route marker at a junction. What do they tell you?
choices: The diamond marks an Interstate and the shield marks a county road
The diamond marks a North Carolina route and the shield marks a U.S. highway
oneLineConcept: Diamond = NC route; shield = U.S. highway
explanation:
Route markers show which road you are on. In North Carolina, a **diamond** marks a **North Carolina route**, a **shield** marks a **U.S. highway**, and a **red, white, and blue shield** marks an **Interstate**.

**Wrong choices**
- Both are warning signs: Route markers are guide signs, not warning signs.
- The diamond marks an Interstate and the shield marks a county road: Interstates use a red, white, and blue shield, not a diamond.
- Both mark toll roads: These shapes show the route system, not tolls.

stem: What does a brown guide sign usually point to?
oneLineConcept: Brown guide signs: parks and recreation
explanation:
**Brown** guide signs lead to **parks, recreation areas, and places of cultural interest**. Green signs give directions, and blue signs show services.

**Wrong choices**
- A hospital: Hospitals are shown on blue and white service signs.
- A construction zone: Construction zones are marked with orange signs.
- A school crossing: School crossings are marked with five-sided yellow-green signs.

stem: You are on a two-lane road and see a diamond sign with two arrows pointing in opposite directions. What should you expect?
choices: The next lane is for passing only
Oncoming traffic will share the road with you
oneLineConcept: Two-way traffic sign: expect oncoming vehicles
explanation:
Two arrows pointing in **opposite directions** on a yellow diamond warn of **two-way traffic** ahead. Expect **oncoming vehicles** and **stay to the right** of the center line.

**Wrong choices**
- The next lane is for passing only: The sign does not set aside a passing lane.
- The road becomes one-way: The sign warns of the opposite: traffic will move both ways.
- You must turn around: The sign is a warning, not an order to turn around.

stem: You are driving toward the top of this picture on a divided highway. The solid yellow line is on your right and the solid white line is on your left. What does this tell you?
choices: You are in a two-way left-turn lane
The road is about to narrow
You are traveling the wrong way
You are in the correct lane for passing
oneLineConcept: Yellow edge line on your right = wrong way
explanation:
On a divided highway the **yellow line marks the left edge** and the **white line marks the right edge**. If you see the **reverse**, with yellow on your right, you are **traveling in the wrong direction**. Pull to the shoulder when safe and turn around when the way is clear.

**Wrong choices**
- You are in the correct lane for passing: Passing lanes still have the yellow edge line on the driver's left.
- You are in a two-way left-turn lane: A two-way left-turn lane is in the center of the road, marked with yellow lines on both sides.
- The road is about to narrow: Edge line colors tell you direction, not that the road is narrowing.
imageAlt: A road seen from above with two lanes. A blue car in the left lane has a white arrow pointing toward the top of the picture. The left edge of the road has a solid white line, the right edge has a solid yellow line, and a broken white line separates the two lanes.

stem: You want to turn left. The signal shows a steady red light on top and a green left arrow at the bottom. What may you do?
choices: Turn left with care; this is a protected turn
Turn left only after oncoming traffic has passed, since you must yield to it
Go straight but do not turn
Stop and wait, because the red light controls all turns
oneLineConcept: Green arrow with red ball: protected turn in the arrow's direction
explanation:
When an arrow and a circular light are both shown, **turning traffic follows the arrow** and through traffic follows the circular light. A **green arrow** gives a **protected movement**, so you may **turn left with care** while oncoming traffic is stopped. Drivers going straight must stop for the red light.

**Wrong choices**
- Stop and wait, because the red light controls all turns: The arrow, not the red light, controls the left turn.
- Go straight but do not turn: The red light means through traffic must stop.
- Turn left only after oncoming traffic has passed, since you must yield to it: That describes a flashing yellow arrow; a green arrow means oncoming traffic is held.
imageAlt: A traffic signal with four lights stacked vertically. The top light is a lit red circle. The two middle lights are dark. The bottom light is a lit green arrow pointing left.

stem: You want to turn right. The light is steady red and this sign is posted next to it. What must you do?
choices: Stop, then turn right when the way is clear
Turn right only if no pedestrians are present
Stay stopped until the light turns green
oneLineConcept: NO TURN ON RED: stay stopped until green
explanation:
Normally you may turn right on red after a full stop. This sign reads **NO TURN ON RED**, so you must **stay stopped until the light turns green**, even if the way is clear.

**Wrong choices**
- Stop, then turn right when the way is clear: That is the usual rule, but this sign takes it away.
- Turn right without stopping: You may never turn on red without stopping first, and here you may not turn at all.
- Turn right only if no pedestrians are present: The sign forbids the turn whether or not people are crossing.
imageAlt: A traffic signal with three lights stacked vertically; the top red light is lit and the others are dark. Beside it is a white rectangular sign with black letters reading NO TURN ON RED.

imageSource.title: MUTCD (FHWA) sign R10-11a beside a standard traffic signal
